opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is: usually a lot less than people assume. A video is a curated sample, and the first thing I try to figure out is how much curation went into it. Was this the first take or the fiftieth? Is it one continuous shot, or are there cuts right at the moments where things would be hardest? If there's a cut just before the robot grasps an object or just after it recovers from a slip, that's where I'd want to see the footage.

Then there's the question of autonomy. Is the robot actually making its own decisions, or is someone teleoperating it off camera, or is it replaying a trajectory that was tuned for exactly that scene? Teleoperation isn't cheating if it's disclosed. It's a legitimate way to collect data and show what the hardware can do. But it tells you about the hardware, not about the intelligence, and those are very different claims.

I also look at the environment. If everything is perfectly lit, the objects are in exactly the same place, and the floor is flat and clean, you're seeing the robot in its comfort zone. The interesting question is always how it behaves when something changes, like a push, a different object, or a slippery surface. Coming from locomotion, that's something we care about a lot. A walking demo on a flat lab floor is nice, but a robot getting kicked, stumbling, and catching itself tells you much more about how robust the policy really is.

And speed matters. A lot of manipulation videos are sped up, sometimes four or eight times, and that's fine as long as it's labeled. But it hides how slow and hesitant the system really is.

So when I watch a video, I'm really trying to reconstruct the distribution behind it. What's the success rate, how many conditions was it tested in, and what happens in the failures? The most convincing demos I've seen are the long, unedited ones, or the ones that deliberately show the failures alongside the successes. That's when you start to trust that what you're seeing is representative and not the one good run out of a hundred.

r001.rationale: The response examines how the demo may have been produced, including cuts, teleoperation, or replaying a trajectory tuned for that scene.

r002.rationale: It explicitly asks whether someone is teleoperating the robot off camera.

r003.rationale: It mentions teleoperation but does not explain imitation learning from extensive human teleoperation data collected under matching conditions.

r004.rationale: It discusses robustness to changed conditions but does not identify the misleading impression that demo success means the robot can handle arbitrary tasks in an unfamiliar home.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because I've been on both sides of it. I've made those videos, and I've also sat there watching other people's videos trying to figure out what's real. And the honest answer is that a video alone tells you surprisingly little. It tells you that at least once, under conditions you don't know, the robot did the thing. That's really the floor of what you can conclude.

So the first thing I look for is what's not in the frame. Is there an operator just off camera? Is there a tether? A lot of legged robot demos, especially a few years ago, were teleoperated or at least had a human providing high-level commands, and the video is cut so that the human is invisible. That's not necessarily dishonest, but it changes completely what the demo means. A robot walking over rubble because a person is steering every step is a mechanical achievement, not an autonomy achievement.

The second thing is cuts. If there's a cut between the robot approaching an obstacle and the robot being past the obstacle, I mentally discount that entirely. One continuous take is worth more than ten edited sequences. And related to that, I want to know how many attempts it took. We've all shot the twenty takes and kept the one. When I see a result I care about, I'll go ask the authors directly: what's the success rate, how many trials, what's the failure mode. The people doing serious work are usually very happy to tell you, because they know the number and they're a bit frustrated that the video doesn't convey it.

Third is how much the environment was prepared. Is the terrain something the robot was trained on specifically, or something it's never seen? With learned controllers this is the big question, because you can get very impressive behavior on the training distribution and have it fall apart with a slightly different surface or a slightly different friction. So when I see a parkour video, I'm asking whether those boxes are at the heights it practiced, or whether someone just dragged furniture into the lab and said go.

And then the last one, which is more subtle: I look at how the robot recovers from small perturbations. A robot that's stiff and perfect is actually less convincing to me than one that stumbles a little and catches itself, because the stumble tells you there's a real feedback loop running, not a replayed trajectory. If the motion looks too clean, I get suspicious.

So what I'd say is a video is a good existence proof and a terrible measurement. It proves the thing is possible. It doesn't tell you the reliability, the generalization, or the autonomy, and those three are what actually matter if you want to deploy something. That's why I push for releasing code and for showing failures, which, to be fair, we've gotten better at as a field. But the incentive to post the one clean take is very strong, and I don't think it's going anywhere.

r001.rationale: The response suggests checking for hidden operators, tethers, edits, and prepared terrain, but does not frame the assessment as considering the easiest way to produce the displayed behavior.

r002.rationale: It explicitly asks whether an off-camera operator is steering the robot and explains that human steering changes what the demo demonstrates.

r003.rationale: It discusses teleoperation and learned controllers, but does not say that autonomy may rely on imitation learning from extensive human teleoperation data collected under matching conditions.

r004.rationale: It warns that performance may fail outside the training distribution, but does not identify the impression that the demo proves the robot can handle arbitrary tasks in an unfamiliar home.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to ask what you’re not seeing. A video shows that the robot did something at least once, but it doesn’t tell you how many attempts it took, how much the setup was tuned, or what happens if you change the conditions a little bit.

So I’d want to know: Is this autonomous? Is someone controlling it? How much does the robot know about the environment beforehand? And can it repeat the task reliably? Those are very different claims, even though the videos might look quite similar.

A demonstration can be a useful proof of possibility. But to understand the capability, you need some sense of the failures and the range of conditions where it works. If you move an object or change the terrain, does it adapt, or does everything fall apart? That’s usually much more informative than the most impressive successful run.

r002.rationale: It asks whether someone is controlling the robot, explicitly raising the possibility that a seemingly autonomous demonstration is actually human-controlled.

r003.rationale: It does not mention imitation learning, extensive human teleoperation data, or training conditions that closely match the demonstration.

r004.rationale: It discusses adapting to changed objects or terrain, but does not identify the impression that success implies handling arbitrary tasks in an unfamiliar home.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be quite careful, because a video shows you that something worked once. It doesn’t necessarily tell you how often it works, how many attempts it took, or how much effort went into setting up that particular situation.

What I look for is how much variation there is. Does the robot do the same thing in different environments, with different initial conditions? If something goes wrong, can it recover? A longer, continuous sequence can tell you more than a collection of very impressive short clips, because you get to see the transitions and the mistakes.

And then there are things you simply can’t infer from the video: whether there’s a person providing commands, what information the controller has access to, or whether the robot was trained specifically for that setup. So I’d treat the video as evidence that the behavior is possible, but to understand the capability, I’d want to know the conditions and the success rate.

r002.rationale: It says a video cannot establish whether a person is providing commands, communicating the possibility of human control behind the demonstrated behavior.

r003.rationale: It does not mention imitation learning, extensive human teleoperation data, or training under closely matching conditions.

r004.rationale: It recommends checking performance across environments, but does not identify the misleading impression that success implies handling arbitrary tasks in an unfamiliar home.
